{"id": "54:49/q16", "question": "What practical teachings about decree do the cited reports give?", "turns_on": "The different teachings attached to reports about decree.", "positions": [{"id": "54:49/q16/p1", "position": "Everything, including incapacity and ability, occurs by decree.", "reasons": "Tawus heard Companions affirm it; Ibn Umar transmitted the prophetic wording. Ibn Kathir says Muslim alone gives the route through Malik. Ibn Abbas even includes resting one's hand on one's cheek."}, {"id": "54:49/q16/p2", "position": "Belief in good and bad decree is a condition of true faith.", "reasons": "Bursevi and Ibn Kathir report the prophetic enumeration with divine unity, prophethood, death or resurrection, and decree; Ibn Kathir gives Tirmidhi's preferred route and Ibn Majah's transmission. Study Quran cites the condition, and Ibn Kathir reports Ubada's deathbed instruction."}, {"id": "54:49/q16/p3", "position": "Accept what God apportions and still seek His help and act.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir calls the prophetic counsel sound: avoid helplessness and if-only regret that opens Satan's work. The Prophet told Ibn Abbas that no combined human benefit or harm exceeds the decree and that pens and scrolls are finished. Abu Hurayra reports that belief removes worry and grief."}]}
{"id": "54:49/q17", "question": "What do reports say about deniers of decree?", "turns_on": "Which reported sanction or eschatological consequence is in view.", "positions": [{"id": "54:49/q17/p1", "position": "They are the community's Magians, and believers should not visit their sick or attend their funerals.", "reasons": "Aisha's report is ungraded by Razi. Qurtubi attributes wording via Jabir to Ibn Majah; Ibn Kathir gives Ibn Umar's route through Ahmad and says none of the six canonical compilers included it. Durr and Alusi record further routes; Study Quran notes Ash'arite citation. Ibn Umar also wrote a Syrian correspondent cutting off contact after learning he disputed decree."}, {"id": "54:49/q17/p2", "position": "They have no share in Islam or the Prophet's intercession.", "reasons": "Anas's report says the Prophet disowns those claiming good and evil are in human hands and denies them intercession. Another report includes the Murji'a as a second group without share in Islam; Alusi says Tirmidhi grades an Ibn Abbas route hasan."}, {"id": "54:49/q17/p3", "position": "Ibn Umar dissociated from deniers, and their spending is not accepted until belief in decree.", "reasons": "Qurtubi cites Muslim for the dissociation, infers a judgment of unbelief, reports Ibn Umar's Uhud-sized gold oath, and compares 9:54 on rejected spending by unbelievers."}, {"id": "54:49/q17/p4", "position": "They face severe punishment or metamorphosis.", "reasons": "Wahidi reports Ka'b saying the Torah predicts their face-down dragging in Fire. Ibn Kathir records Ibn Umar's prophecy of metamorphosis among deniers and heretics, graded hasan sahih gharib by Tirmidhi. Ibn Abbas calls deniers the community's worst, bars visiting or praying for them, threatens physical punishment, and associates the coming error with denial of decreed good and evil. Alusi preserves an Ibn Abbas threat and his statement that adultery, theft, and wine drinking occur by decree. Abu Dharr's report calls disputants with God to account on Judgment Day."}]}
{"id": "54:49/q18", "question": "Does creation by measure require divine wisdom or philosophical necessity?", "turns_on": "Whether wisdom describes the benefits and order of God's act or constrains His act as an antecedent necessity.", "positions": [{"id": "54:49/q18/p1", "position": "Each created thing is proportioned for a wise purpose, including just recompense.", "reasons": "Al-Jubba'i says nothing is aimless and punishment fits deserts. Ibn Ashur connects ordered creation and Judgment through 13:8, 23:115, 15:85-86, and 44:38-40. Tabatabai says an act may be explained through creatures' benefits, as 5:82 and 2:61 illustrate, or through a fitting divine name, as 29:60 and 2:37 illustrate; the punishment here is an instance of a general measured rule. He says reasoning from regular effects, such as eating and drinking, avoids circularity. Study Quran reports precision and purpose stressed by Tabrisī and wisdom by Zamakhshari."}, {"id": "54:49/q18/p2", "position": "God's acts are not governed by an external rational rule or natural necessity.", "reasons": "Tabatabai says general rules are inferred from divine acts, not prior causes governing God, citing 21:23, 22:18, and 2:147. Razi rejects philosophers who make differences depend only on matter's receptivity, since God's will could change sizes and results."}, {"id": "54:49/q18/p3", "position": "The present world is the best possible arrangement.", "reasons": "Bursevi reports Ghazali's argument that a better possible world left unrealized would imply miserliness or incapacity in God."}]}
{"id": "54:49/q19", "question": "How does the verse connect with the surrounding passage?", "turns_on": "Whether it directly explains the preceding punishment, opens the creation-and-command statement, or frames the surah's closing warning.", "positions": [{"id": "54:49/q19/p1", "position": "It gives the reason criminals are made to taste Saqar: they denied decree or meet a measured punishment.", "reasons": "Tabari calls the verse a threat to decree-deniers; Razi reports the common link with 54:48. Muqatil and Wahidi connect the appointed punishment to what precedes. Tabatabai says the criminals' rejection of prophetic guidance carries its measured outcome in 54:47-49. Ibn Ashur says the warnings culminate in purposeful recompense between 54:43 and 54:51; Elmalili says sin cannot be transformed into felicity."}, {"id": "54:49/q19/p2", "position": "It begins a fresh declaration of God's creation, continued by the next verse on His single swift command.", "reasons": "Razi prefers this because 54:50 parallels creation and command in 7:54. He explains that the Prophet's citation of the punishment verses could end before the full final clause, just as partial verses in 4:29, 6:121, and 2:283 are cited. Nasafi and Ibn Ashur link measure to the next statement of swift command."}, {"id": "54:49/q19/p3", "position": "The close warns Quraysh that the measured fate of earlier nations also awaits them.", "reasons": "Islahi says the closing section contrasts worldly humiliation, worse otherworldly punishment, and the God-fearing's reward. He says Quraysh's respite follows the measured rule applied to nations."}, {"id": "54:49/q19/p4", "position": "The verse's measured creation and the next verse display the unconstrained speed and extent of God's power.", "reasons": "Kuran Yolu says no outside power determines God's will and neither time nor place confines Him."}]}
{"id": "54:49/q20", "question": "What inward lesson is drawn from the verse?", "turns_on": "Which devotional or metaphysical consequence the measured order yields.", "positions": [{"id": "54:49/q20/p1", "position": "Surrender to the settled measure brings trust, acceptance, and release from anxious planning.", "reasons": "Yusuf ibn al-Husayn says decree overcomes resolve; Bursevi's Persian couplet invokes the dried pen and counsels silence before the eternal Tablet. Study Quran reports Ibn Ajibah's appeal to 102:5 and 40:44 for accepting every decree and relief from sorrow."}, {"id": "54:49/q20/p2", "position": "Finding God outweighs possession of every created thing.", "reasons": "Study Quran reports al-Maybudi's maxim: the one who finds God has everything, whereas someone deprived of Him has nothing despite possessing all."}, {"id": "54:49/q20/p3", "position": "True freedom emerges through surrender of ego, while human choice itself manifests God-given capacity.", "reasons": "Study Quran reports Sufi readings relating the Divine Names al-Murid and al-Qadir to humanity's capacity, citing 2:31; will is divine power manifested and freedom arises through surrender. Ibn Arabi's saints, most capable of miracles, least use them because they accept God's will. Other Sufis identify a person's lot with an essence known before creation and relate freedom to the breathed Spirit in Adam, 32:9. Bursevi's Najmiyya reading measures all scientific and concrete being by original disposition and capacity, citing 20:50."}]}
{"id": "54:49/q21", "question": "Can another agent determine a thing's measure?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "54:49/q21/p1", "position": "No agent other than God can impose the measure of a thing as it pleases.", "reasons": "Elmalili denies that any other agent can determine or necessitate the measure at will."}]}
{"id": "54:49/q22", "question": "What follows for those who disbelieve in divine decree?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "54:49/q22/p1", "position": "They can be punished for denying it.", "reasons": "Al-Nahhas says the verse demonstrates punishment for disbelief in divine decree."}]}
{"id": "54:49/q23", "question": "How is the report that all ability is decreed used against deniers?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "54:49/q23/p1", "position": "It refutes the Qadariyya.", "reasons": "Qurtubi explicitly presents the report as a refutation of the Qadariyya."}]}
{"id": "54:49/q24", "question": "Why did this verse become central to debates over choice?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "54:49/q24/p1", "position": "The Prophet's dispute with deniers of decree made it a focus of the dispute over divine determinism and human choice.", "reasons": "Study Quran connects the debate with the reported prophetic encounter."}]}

{"id": "55:26/q02", "question": "What does the pronoun in عَلَيْهَا refer to?", "turns_on": "Whether context recalls the earlier earth, supplies the wider world, or points back to the ships; Razi invokes 55:27 for earth.", "positions": [{"id": "55:26/q02/p1", "position": "The earth.", "reasons": "Wahidi-Basit, Qurtubi, Abu Hayyan, Samin, and Elmalili cite its earlier mention at 55:10; Nahhas relates it to the earth God spread out. Tabrisi, Ibn Jawzi, Razi, Burhan, Itqan, Bursevi, Ibn Ashur, and Asad allow context to supply an unnamed earth. Tabrisi compares a Medinan expression about two lava tracts; Razi cites 35:45; Samin reports 38:32 as an analogy but also the objection that 55:10 already names earth; Ibn Ashur likewise cites 38:32. Razi says 55:27 favors earth over ships."}, {"id": "55:26/q02/p2", "position": "The world, inferred from a previously mentioned part.", "reasons": "Burhan attributes this to Ibn Malik; Itqan says context can supply 'earth or world' without a named antecedent and compares the unnamed deceased in an inheritance expression."}, {"id": "55:26/q02/p3", "position": "The ships just mentioned.", "reasons": "Razi reports that everyone aboard is near destruction and cannot control benefit or harm, while judging the earth reading better because of 55:27."}, {"id": "55:26/q02/p4", "position": "The whole universe.", "reasons": "Asad reports Ibn Kathir's extension to the heavens as implying this antecedent."}]}
{"id": "55:26/q03", "question": "Why say عَلَيْهَا rather than 'in the earth'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "55:26/q03/p1", "position": "Being 'upon' it suggests no settled permanence at annihilation.", "reasons": "Burhan explicitly contrasts this wording with 'in the earth.'"}]}
{"id": "55:26/q04", "question": "How can كُلُّ مَنْ عَلَيْهَا be grammatically construed?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "55:26/q04/p1", "position": "The relative من can be modified by either a single word or a clause.", "reasons": "Burhan gives one reading of the expression as 'every person established upon it.'"}]}
{"id": "55:26/q05", "question": "In what sense and at what time is each being فَانٍ?", "turns_on": "Whether فَانٍ anticipates death, describes present contingency, or denotes extinction versus transition; Razi disputes an inference about bodily persistence.", "positions": [{"id": "55:26/q05/p1", "position": "They are destined to die or pass away in the future.", "reasons": "Ibn Jawzi glosses the word as doomed to perish. Razi compares the living Prophet called dead at 39:30 and ordinary speech treating the near future as arrived. Ibn Ashur says the active participle has future sense and cites 39:30. Tabatabai says this marks the end of earthly life and onset of the next; Ibn Ashur adds reckoning and recompense."}, {"id": "55:26/q05/p2", "position": "Created beings are already perishing through contingent, changing existence.", "reasons": "Razi says human existence is an accident alternating origination and nonexistence; he rejects the inference that a body cannot persist two moments, since man includes transient accidents even if the body remains. Biqai says every creature lies between nonexistence before creation and after extinction and its states, qualities, and powers are continually made and unmade, with hidden destructive causes like those around ship passengers. Bursevi reports that dependent existence is not truly self-subsisting; real existence belongs to the pre-eternal."}, {"id": "55:26/q05/p3", "position": "Perishing is extinction or passage out of existence.", "reasons": "Tabrisi says earthly creatures pass out of existence. Abu Hayyan applies extinction to every created thing, cites 28:88, and says 'face' means reality without bodily limbs."}, {"id": "55:26/q05/p4", "position": "Perishing is departure from this world and return to God, not absolute annihilation.", "reasons": "Tabatabai says many verses explain it as return; the next life begins for earthly inhabitants."}, {"id": "55:26/q05/p5", "position": "Bodies themselves cannot persist for two moments.", "reasons": "Razi rejects this inference from the verse: a human includes changing accidents, but the body may remain and is not literally the whole human."}]}
{"id": "55:26/q06", "question": "What accounts for the form فَانٍ?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "55:26/q06/p1", "position": "An original yāʾ was silenced for heaviness and then deleted before the still tanwīn.", "reasons": "Nahhas gives this morphological sequence."}]}
{"id": "55:26/q07", "question": "What did the angels infer when this verse was revealed?", "turns_on": "The reported later verse differs, as does Bursevi's qualification about kinds of angelic spirit.", "positions": [{"id": "55:26/q07/p1", "position": "They thought earth's people had perished, then learned their own mortality from 28:88.", "reasons": "Wahidi-Basit transmits this from al-Kalbi and Muqatil; Qurtubi attributes it to Ibn Abbas and Muqatil. The first report says earth's people; the second says its inhabitants."}, {"id": "55:26/q07/p2", "position": "They thought Adam's children had perished, then learned their own mortality from 3:185.", "reasons": "Bursevi reports that subtle angelic bodies and attached spirits perish, while lofty immaterial spirits do not."}]}
{"id": "55:26/q08", "question": "Should recitation stop after the statement of perishing?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "55:26/q08/p1", "position": "Continue through the statement that the Lord's Face remains in 55:27.", "reasons": "Al-Shaʿbi is reported by Wahidi-Basit, Ibn Kathir, Durr, Itqan, and Nashr; Itqan says Ibn Abi Hatim recorded it. {"id": "55:26/q09", "question": "Which sakt and madd combinations does Nashr transmit or rule out?", "turns_on": "The transmitted reader, hamza environment, and whether madd entails sakt.", "positions": [{"id": "55:26/q09/p1", "position": "Ibn Dhakwan's sakt occurs with either long or medium madd.", "reasons": "Nashr says both combinations are transmitted."}, {"id": "55:26/q09/p2", "position": "For Hafs, sakt requires madd, while qasr occurs only with idraj.", "reasons": "Nashr cites al-Ashnani from Ubayd for the former and al-Fil from Amr for the latter."}, {"id": "55:26/q09/p3", "position": "For Hamza, the options vary by hamza setting and word.", "reasons": "Nashr says easing within one word cancels sakt or tahqiq; across words the separated hamza's easing rules apply. On al-ard and al-insan, naql or sakt occurs; on qad aflaha, man amana, qul uhiya, qalu amanna, fi anfusikum, and ma unzila, sakt, no sakt, and naql occur; ya ayyuha and ha'ula' allow tahqiq or easing without sakt."}, {"id": "55:26/q09/p4", "position": "Hamza's madd must accompany sakt in the relevant settings.", "reasons": "Nashr rejects the apparent Khallad report of madd on shay' without sakt: madd there functions as sakt, whether on the definite article alone or also on separated madd."}, {"id": "55:26/q09/p5", "position": "Khallad permits madd on shay' without sakt.", "reasons": "Nashr reports this apparent transmission only to disallow it."}]}

{"id": "55:26/q11", "question": "Why is mortality mentioned among divine favors?", "turns_on": "Whether the announcement's warning and transition to reward make death a favor, or the refrain attaches elsewhere.", "positions": [{"id": "55:26/q11/p1", "position": "Its warning and consequences are favors.", "reasons": "Baghawi says admonition and restraint deter sin and explain the refrain. Tabrisi says death equalizes creatures, leads to reward, warns of worldly limits, and preserves moral agency because immediate reward would compel obedience and erase merit. Qurtubi separately gives equality and transfer to recompense. Itqan adds relief from a troubled abode and from wicked people for the righteous. Tabatabai calls worldly life preliminary to afterlife and explicitly answers the objection that perishing cannot be a favor."}, {"id": "55:26/q11/p2", "position": "Perishing itself is not a favor, and the refrain is not a tailpiece to this statement.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur denies both connections."}]}

{"id": "55:26/q14", "question": "What does the contrast with the enduring Lord teach?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "55:26/q14/p1", "position": "Created things perish while God alone endures.", "reasons": "Tab-Full says His Face remains with majesty and honor; Ibn Kathir says the Lord is ever-living and never dies. Abu Hayyan says Face denotes divine reality, not a bodily limb. Burhan says the Lord's enduring Face does not conflict with earthly mortality. Islahi says all other beings perish; Study Quran cites 28:88 and says divine endurance offsets the passage's dualities. Biqai argues all besides God is contingent, and Islahi connects the created order to final judgment."}]}
{"id": "55:26/q15", "question": "What rhetorical figure joins this verse to the next?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "55:26/q15/p1", "position": "Iftinan combines consolation for mortal creatures with praise of God's abiding majesty.", "reasons": "Itqan says the two modes occur in ten words and cites 19:72, which joins gladness and consolation, as another example."}]}
{"id": "55:26/q16", "question": "What inward meanings are given to perishing here?", "turns_on": "The reported inward interpretations apply perishing to desire, spiritual faculties, voluntary transformation, or ontological dependence.", "positions": [{"id": "55:26/q16/p1", "position": "A person between the two ends of annihilation is perishing.", "reasons": "Sulami transmits this from Junayd."}, {"id": "55:26/q16/p2", "position": "One who keeps following desire perishes without realizing it.", "reasons": "Sulami transmits this from Ibn Ata."}, {"id": "55:26/q16/p3", "position": "Knowing annihilation and abiding means knowing this world's passing and the afterlife's permanence.", "reasons": "Sulami attributes this definition to unnamed authorities."}, {"id": "55:26/q16/p4", "position": "Those aboard sailing vessels reach God by annihilation in Him.", "reasons": "Qashani applies the preceding ship image inwardly."}, {"id": "55:26/q16/p5", "position": "Every faculty and station on the body's earth vanishes upon reaching the goal.", "reasons": "Qashani names spirit, intellect, heart, soul, and their stations and ranks as the particulars."}, {"id": "55:26/q16/p6", "position": "Perishing is natural death in sensual pleasures or voluntary death by shedding human traits.", "reasons": "Bursevi contrasts bodily immersion with taking on spiritual qualities; he also says sound intellect passes from natural conditions into divine manifestations."}, {"id": "55:26/q16/p7", "position": "The universe is already perishing to deeper discernment because dependent being lacks self-subsistence.", "reasons": "Bursevi transmits this from unnamed authorities and reserves real existence for the pre-eternal."}]}
{"id": "55:27/q01", "question": "What remains when those on earth perish?", "turns_on": "Whether perishing is read as future death or as the present dependence of created existence.", "positions": [{"id": "55:27/q01/p1", "position": "God alone remains eternally, while every creature passes away.", "reasons": "Muqatil compares 28:88; Tabari specifies jinn and humans; Abu Hayyan says every created thing is extinguished; Islahi links creation, provision, wisdom and sovereignty to its end and subsequent judgment; Ibn Ashur says mortality points to reckoning; Kuranyolu draws a call to live for God's pleasure."}, {"id": "55:27/q01/p2", "position": "The universe is already perishing in its dependence, even while it appears to exist.", "reasons": "Bursevi reports that dependent things lack self-subsisting existence; only the pre-eternal is real."}]}
{"id": "55:27/q02", "question": "What does 'the face of your Lord' denote here?", "turns_on": "Whether face refers directly to God, an attribute or manifestation, or the Godward aspect and deeds of creation.", "positions": [{"id": "55:27/q02/p1", "position": "God Himself, His enduring Essence or Reality.", "reasons": "Muqatil cites 28:88. Nahhas compares 'face of the earth'; Tabarsi cites the face as the person's manifestation through proofs and Arabic idioms for the essence of an opinion or plan, including al-A'sha's poetry. Razi says seeing a face lets one know the whole person; Qurtubi cites Ibn Abbas, Ibn Furak and Abu al-Ma'ali; Biqai says the face, the noblest part, cannot endure apart from its possessor. Bursevi calls it a borrowing from the chief seat of the senses; Asad, Ibn Ashur and Islahi cite ordinary metonymy. Baydawi and Bursevi also describe the God-facing aspect of otherwise finite things. Elmalili says nominative dhu supports the Essence and excludes created relations."}, {"id": "55:27/q02/p2", "position": "God as manifest through His signs and proofs.", "reasons": "Wahidi's meaning scholars liken signs to a human face making a person apparent; Tabarsi combines this with reference to God Himself; Qurtubi reports it as an alternative."}, {"id": "55:27/q02/p3", "position": "The Godward direction, aim, or aspect of beings, including the means of drawing near to Him.", "reasons": "Tabrisi cites poetry joining God's face to deeds; Qurtubi reports the approach to God; Bursevi's Ibn al-Shaykh links direction with 'in God's side' (39:56), while Sa'di al-Mufti explains the aim as a genitive. Baydawi's Godward aspect is reported by Alusi and Elmalili; Shihab calls direction an alternative to essence. Tabatabai says this can encompass prophets, saints, religion, reward and nearness. Alusi objects that a deed reading does not fit universal perishing."}, {"id": "55:27/q02/p4", "position": "Righteous deeds directed to God, or their enduring reward.", "reasons": "Bursevi's Ibn al-Shaykh says only God-directed works escape passing; Elmalili says a deed is kept until its reward, which remains in its place. {"id": "55:27/q03", "question": "Can the divine 'face' be understood as a bodily organ?", "turns_on": "Whether to leave the nonbodily expression unprobed or explain its figurative meaning.", "positions": [{"id": "55:27/q03/p1", "position": "No; divine transcendence rules out a corporeal face.", "reasons": "Razi argues from 28:88 that if face were an organ, other divine parts would perish; he says essence includes attributes, as a remaining garment includes color and size. {"id": "55:27/q04", "question": "Do God's attributes remain with His Essence?", "turns_on": "Whether the attributes belong with the Essence in what the verse calls enduring.", "positions": [{"id": "55:27/q04/p1", "position": "Yes; the enduring Essence includes its attributes.", "reasons": "Razi's garment analogy says the thing that remains retains color and dimensions; Qashani expressly includes all attributes; Ibn Ashur says the majesty-and-generosity qualification embraces transcendence, perfection, beauty and beneficence."}, {"id": "55:27/q04/p2", "position": "Only the divine Essence remains; distinct attributes pass away.", "reasons": "Study Quran reports the inference made by theologians separating Essence from Attributes, and reports Razi's objection that such a claim would require the wording 'nothing remains except the Face of thy Lord.'"}]}
{"id": "55:27/q05", "question": "To whom does 'your Lord' address the verse?", "turns_on": "Whether the singular address names the Prophet in particular or distributes the warning to each listener.", "positions": [{"id": "55:27/q05/p1", "position": "Every hearer is addressed.", "reasons": "Razi says each person must attend to God alone; the singular prevents a pair of addressees from exempting each other. {"id": "55:27/q06", "question": "What does the word 'Lord' convey here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "55:27/q06/p1", "position": "The one who nurtures and sustains.", "reasons": "Razi reports rabb as a verbal noun for upbringing, by comparison with verbs of raising; alternatively it is an agent-like adjective from that noun. {"id": "55:27/q07", "question": "Why say 'the face of your Lord' rather than simply 'your Lord' or another divine name?", "turns_on": "Which force of the chosen expression the commentator emphasizes.", "positions": [{"id": "55:27/q07/p1", "position": "The wording asserts God's absolute permanence without implying that a subject remains under His lordship.", "reasons": "Razi says Lord, Creator and Provider are agent names that could suggest continuing objects; even Allah may be explained as the worshipped one. Elmalili says face stresses the Essence's permanence as its attributes and lordship manifest."}, {"id": "55:27/q07/p2", "position": "The face, as the noblest part, more eloquently conveys the whole enduring person.", "reasons": "Biqai says a face cannot continue apart from its possessor and its mention is more eloquent than mentioning the possessor directly."}, {"id": "55:27/q07/p3", "position": "The wording evokes care, gentleness and the sūrah's blessings.", "reasons": "Razi contrasts the gentleness of direct address to the Lord with the might of abiding; Study Quran reports that 'your Lord' suits the recurring blessing and bounty theme."}, {"id": "55:27/q07/p4", "position": "This passage's lordly sustaining favors suit 'your Lord'; other passages use 'face of Allah' for worship or charity.", "reasons": "Razi compares 2:115 and 30:38. {"id": "55:27/q08", "question": "How is 'rabb' ordinarily constructed in Arabic?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "55:27/q08/p1", "position": "It is ordinarily annexed; when unannexed it is accompanied by another description.", "reasons": "Razi cites 44:8, 1:2, 34:15 and 36:58."}]}
{"id": "55:27/q09", "question": "Is 'rabb' originally a verbal noun or a derived description?", "turns_on": "Its proposed morphological origin.", "positions": [{"id": "55:27/q09/p1", "position": "It may be a verbal noun meaning upbringing.", "reasons": "Razi compares verbs meaning to raise or nurture."}, {"id": "55:27/q09/p2", "position": "It may be a derived adjective meaning one who nurtures.", "reasons": "Razi compares agent names and qualities formed from verbal nouns."}]}
{"id": "55:27/q10", "question": "How is ذُو read, and what does it modify?", "turns_on": "The case ending and whether the epithet follows face, Lord, or an implied predicate.", "positions": [{"id": "55:27/q10/p1", "position": "The common nominative ذُو modifies وَجْهُ.", "reasons": "Tabari, Nahhas, Wahidi, Jishumi, Abu Hayyan, Samin, Nasafi, Elmalili and Study Quran attach the adjective to face; Wahidi says a Lord adjunct would require ذِي. {"id": "55:27/q11", "question": "What further recitational variants affect the epithet?", "turns_on": "Which occurrence or pronunciation the report concerns.", "positions": [{"id": "55:27/q11/p1", "position": "At the sūrah's ending the seven readers differ in the corresponding phrase.", "reasons": "Al-Samin notes the contrast with this occurrence."}, {"id": "55:27/q11/p2", "position": "Reports differ on Ibn Dhakwan's imāla in الإكرام.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazari says al-Tajrid records only imāla through al-Akhfash and several transmitters, alongside عمران (3:36) and إكراههن (24:33)."}]}
{"id": "55:27/q12", "question": "What does 'majesty' mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether majesty is glossed chiefly as greatness, independence, or awe-inspiring transcendence.", "positions": [{"id": "55:27/q12/p1", "position": "Divine greatness, exaltation, sovereignty and deservingness of praise.", "reasons": "Wahidi and Qurtubi derive jalal from jalla, to be great; Tabarsi adds supreme beneficence as the source of favors; Ibn Abbas is reported in Ibn Kathir and Durr as glossing it greatness and pride. {"id": "55:27/q15", "question": "What does the combined title 'Possessor of Majesty and Honor' express?", "turns_on": "How the two qualities divide between transcendence, positive perfection, God's action, and human response.", "positions": [{"id": "55:27/q15/p1", "position": "It joins God's transcendent greatness with generous beneficence.", "reasons": "Baydawi calls these absolute self-sufficiency and general bounty; Bursevi and Alusi pair independence with complete favor; Ibn Ashur says the pair covers transcendence, perfection, beauty and service to creatures; Study Quran relates the pair to Majesty and Beauty."}, {"id": "55:27/q15/p2", "position": "The title can mark God's worthiness of reverence and His honoring of servants respectively.", "reasons": "Ibn Jawzi allows one noun to name a divine attribute and the other a servant's act, comparing 74:56; Abu Hayyan reports God as the giver of majesty and honor to sincere servants."}, {"id": "55:27/q15/p3", "position": "Majesty denotes negated limitations; generosity or beauty denotes affirmed perfections.", "reasons": "Alusi reports al-Kirmani's examples of no partner versus life and knowledge, but says the division needs examination. Study Quran reports a Shiite scheme of Beauty's inherent positive attributes and Majesty's denial of bodily limits."}, {"id": "55:27/q15/p4", "position": "The name ultimately denotes the sacred Essence.", "reasons": "Tabatabai says the paired names of majesty and beauty name God Himself, comparing 55:78."}, {"id": "55:27/q15/p5", "position": "It is among God's uniquely exalted names.", "reasons": "Alusi and Elmalili report Raghib's description of the full title as unique to God and one of His greatest descriptions."}]}
{"id": "55:27/q16", "question": "What is reported about invoking God by this title?", "turns_on": "The reports concern distinct exhortations, answered prayers and transmitted formulas.", "positions": [{"id": "55:27/q16/p1", "position": "The Prophet urges persistent repetition of 'O Possessor of Majesty and Honor' in supplication.", "reasons": "Qurtubi transmits Anas and an Ibn Mas'ud attribution; Abu Ubayd explains ilzaz as adhering and insistent prayer. {"id": "55:27/q17", "question": "How does the verse relate to the death of creatures?", "turns_on": "Whether the point is the coming end and judgment or why that end counts as a favor.", "positions": [{"id": "55:27/q17/p1", "position": "The verse states a universal end and anticipates reckoning and reward.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir reports Qatada that God tells of creation and then its passing; Ibn Ashur says the reminder of death looks ahead to recompense; Islahi says none can challenge God's judgment or intercede without leave."}, {"id": "55:27/q17/p2", "position": "Death is a favor because it leads from earthly trial to recompense.", "reasons": "Tabrisi says death equalizes creatures and warns of life's end; immediate reward would compel action and deprive it of merit. {"id": "55:27/q18", "question": "What did the angels conclude when the verse was revealed?", "turns_on": "The report differs on the later verse and on what exactly perishes.", "positions": [{"id": "55:27/q18/p1", "position": "They first inferred the earthly beings had perished, then learned their own mortality from 28:88.", "reasons": "Muqatil says they wondered how life could benefit people and were reassured that all die; Wahidi attributes the report to al-Kalbi and Muqatil."}, {"id": "55:27/q18/p2", "position": "They first thought Adam's children had perished, then learned their own mortality from 'every soul tastes death' (3:185).", "reasons": "Bursevi adds that angels' subtle bodies and attached spirits perish but lofty immaterial spirits do not."}]}
{"id": "55:27/q19", "question": "Where should a reciter pause across verses 26–27?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "55:27/q19/p1", "position": "Continue past 'all on earth perish' until God's abiding face has been recited.", "reasons": "Wahidi, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jazari, Durr and Suyuti transmit al-Sha'bi's direction; Suyuti cites Ibn Abi Hatim. {"id": "55:27/q20", "question": "How does this verse connect to other Qur'anic passages?", "turns_on": "Which passage supplies the comparison: 28:88 or the sūrah's own ending.", "positions": [{"id": "55:27/q20/p1", "position": "It parallels 28:88: all things perish except God's face.", "reasons": "Muqatil, Razi, Abu Hayyan, Ibn Kathir, Elmalili, Asad and Study Quran invoke the parallel; Ibn Kathir also connects seeking the face to 18:28 and 76:9."}, {"id": "55:27/q20/p2", "position": "The closing title in 55:78 echoes 55:27 and confirms God's exclusive exaltation.", "reasons": "Islahi says no partner shares majesty and bounty; Study Quran says the echo places God beyond earthly and heavenly blessings; Tabatabai also compares 55:78."}]}
{"id": "55:27/q21", "question": "What role does this verse play in the sūrah's movement?", "turns_on": "Which structural connection within the sūrah is emphasized.", "positions": [{"id": "55:27/q21/p1", "position": "It closes the worldly blessings and turns toward the Hereafter.", "reasons": "Study Quran locates the turn after vv. 10–25; Abu Hayyan contrasts the passing world and enduring face with the sūrah's later lasting Paradise and blessed name; Bursevi says generosity after death includes resurrection and eternal bliss."}, {"id": "55:27/q21/p2", "position": "It sets God's permanence against creation's transient dualities and grounds the repeated favor refrain.", "reasons": "Study Quran contrasts God with what passes; Ibn Ashur says the ensuing question about favors follows because His great and generous treatment never ceases; Islahi traces the passage to the earth since verse 10."}]}
{"id": "55:27/q22", "question": "What rhetorical effect joins human death to divine permanence?", "turns_on": "The notes identify distinct rhetorical effects of the same juxtaposition.", "positions": [{"id": "55:27/q22/p1", "position": "The sequence blends consolation of creatures and praise of God's enduring majesty and generosity.", "reasons": "Suyuti calls the ten-word turn iftinan, combining two modes, consolation and praise."}, {"id": "55:27/q22/p2", "position": "The verse names a part, 'face,' for the whole divine Self.", "reasons": "Suyuti compares body-wide states expressed through faces and hands and actions of prayer naming whole prayer, citing 2:144, 88:8, 88:3, 2:286, 2:184, 17:78, 76:26, 2:43 and 5:95."}, {"id": "55:27/q22/p3", "position": "God's majesty and generosity signal that kindness c

{"id": "55:27/q23", "question": "What inward insight does the enduring face convey?", "turns_on": "Whether the inward lesson concerns veiling, witnessing, or the paired manifestations.", "positions": [{"id": "55:27/q23/p1", "position": "Divine disclosure and veiling govern what creatures can witness.", "reasons": "Sulami's al-Wasiti says God inwardly discloses in this life while veiling by wonders; in the next He gives outwardly but shields creatures according to their capacity."}, {"id": "55:27/q23/p2", "position": "The knower witnesses God's abiding presence through creation.", "reasons": "Elmalili reports realized knowers who see nothing apart from God; Ibn Ata calls creation darkness lit only by divine manifestation and says overlooking God in, before, after or alongside it veils knowledge."}, {"id": "55:27/q23/p3", "position": "Majesty and generosity manifest as overpowering veils and merciful nearness.", "reasons": "Qashani describes luminous and dark veils, dominion, attributes, gentleness and mercy."}]}
{"id": "55:27/q24", "question": "Does 'face' derive from confrontation?", "turns_on": "Which sense is taken as the lexical starting point.", "positions": [{"id": "55:27/q24/p1", "position": "No; the organ name preceded terms for facing or confrontation.", "reasons": "Razi rejects the reverse derivation found in some legal books and treats later related forms as transferred from the earlier organ word."}, {"id": "55:27/q24/p2", "position": "The original sense may be direction, with essence a later allusion.", "reasons": "Alusi reports this alternative origin account."}]}
{"id": "55:27/q25", "question": "How does the title's majesty-and-generosity description identify the face?", "turns_on": "Whether the modifier attaches semantically to the Essence directly or to a divine name or attribute.", "positions": [{"id": "55:27/q25/p1", "position": "The title identifies God's Essence, which bears these attributes.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur says the epithet embraces transcendence, perfection and beneficence; Elmalili argues that created God-facing relations cannot bear it, so face means Essence."}, {"id": "55:27/q25/p2", "position": "The title can describe a noble divine Name or attribute and thereby ultimately the Essence.", "reasons": "Tabatabai says applying the name to the name ultimately names God; creation's passing leaves the name unchanged."}]}
{"id": "55:27/q26", "question": "How do different accounts of existence frame this verse?", "turns_on": "Whether possible beings possess actual existence or are described as existent through divine manifestation.", "positions": [{"id": "55:27/q26/p1", "position": "Possible beings have actual existence inhering in them.", "reasons": "Alusi identifies this as the view of most philosophers and theologians, in contrast with metaphorical-existence accounts."}, {"id": "55:27/q26/p2", "position": "Created existence is metaphorical, explained either as divine manifestation or as affairs of one Essence.", "reasons": "Alusi distinguishes the theistic philosophers' mirror model from realized Sufis' one-Essence model; his note says the two are often assimilated."}]}
{"id": "55:27/q27", "question": "How is this verse's 'face' compared with other divine attribute expressions?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "55:27/q27/p1", "position": "It serves as a comparison for treating an apparent body-part term as emphatic.", "reasons": "Suyuti reports Mujahid's comparison of the 'hand' in 38:75 with 'the Face of your Lord' here; al-Baghawi rejects the hand-as-addition reading because it would erase Adam's distinction from Satan."}]}
{"id": "55:62/q01", "question": "What does مِن دُونِهِمَا mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether dūn marks lesser rank, addition, proximity, or being before the first pair; comparisons of the garden descriptions inform these readings.", "positions": [{"id": "55:62/q01/p1", "position": "Below the first pair in rank, degree, merit, or standing.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās says lower in degree or rank (al-Naḥḥās, al-Thaʿlabī, al-Wāḥidī, al-Baghawī, Ibn al-Jawzī, al-Qurṭubī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Biqāʿī). Elmalılı renders the pair beyond the preceding one; Iṣlāḥī allows 'besides' and 'in contrast with'; Kur'an Yolu allows two more gardens beyond them.
